strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: while auction collusion literature has extensively studied utility maximizers, this paper is the first to systematically analyze coordination among value-maximizing auto-bidders under RoS constraints, a setting highly relevant to modern ad platforms.

The theoretical results are rigorous and tightly characterized. Theorem 3.1 gives a necessary and sufficient condition (Assumption 1) for coordination to weakly dominate independent bidding in RoS compliance, for any overbidding algorithm -- both directions of the iff are proven with explicit constructions.

Theorem 4.1 shows total-value improvement for mirror-descent algorithms holds unconditionally (no distributional assumption), and Theorem 4.2 shows the simple highest-value-compete rule is asymptotically optimal among *all* coordination mechanisms under Assumption 1 -- a strong and somewhat surprising optimality result.

The extension to non-i.i.d. valuations (Section 5) is a meaningful robustness check, and the paper is honest that individual-level guarantees are lost there, correctly flagging this as an open problem rather than overclaiming.

Experiments cover both symmetric/asymmetric synthetic settings and a real-world dataset (iPinYou), and the reported results (Table 1) consistently corroborate the theory across multiple N and distributional settings, adding empirical credibility to the asymptotic theoretical claims.
Proofs are given in detail in the appendix with clear proof sketches in the main text, aiding verifiability.
weaknesses: The mechanism assumes the coordinator (or coalition) has truthful access to each bidder's private value each round in order to select the highest-value bidder; the paper does not address whether bidders have incentive to truthfully report their values to the coordinator, which is a first-order concern for the practical realizability of the proposed mechanism, especially in the third-party-agent motivating scenario.

The real-world experiment's value model is quite indirect: only winning prices (not actual bidder valuations) are observable in iPinYou, and the paper constructs an i.i.d. value distribution by pooling all winning prices and sampling with replacement, which is a fairly crude proxy that may not reflect realistic value heterogeneity or correlation structure, limiting the strength of the 'real-world validation' claim.

All theory is restricted to (truthful) second-price auctions; many real ad exchanges use first-price or GSP mechanisms where the dominant-strategy argument central to several proofs (e.g., Lemma 3.1) breaks down. This is acknowledged as future work but substantially limits the immediate applicability of the results.

The paper considers only one specific coordination mechanism (highest-value bidder competes, others bid zero); while Theorem 4.2 shows its asymptotic optimality under Assumption 1, no analysis is given for practically motivated alternatives (e.g., partial bid shading, revenue redistribution schemes) that a real bidding agent might prefer for other business reasons (e.g., fairness among advertisers in the coalition, which the paper only briefly mentions as 'redistribution').

Assumption 1 (and Assumption 2) are central to most positive results but can be opaque for practitioners to verify in practice, and the paper's own analysis (Observation 1) shows it is basically guaranteed only for large N, leaving the small-N, non-large-N regime (arguably the most relevant for the third-party agent scenario with few clients) less well covered by guarantees.

There is no explicit discussion of the market-design, antitrust, or platform-policy implications of enabling coordinated bid suppression among competing advertisers, even though this is functionally a form of bid coordination that many ad platforms explicitly prohibit; a brief discussion of these practical/ethical considerations would strengthen the paper's treatment of limitations.
